title: AI music company claims copyright over musician's recording, gets video removed
content:
WTF?! There are worse things AI can do to music streaming services than fill them with slop tracks. Take, for example, the recent case of an AI content company founded last year that claimed ownership of a musician's own five-year-old recording.
As reported by 404 Media, writer and musician Samantha Shokin recorded a 50-second version of Bulgarian folk song Bre Petrunko during the pandemic, initially uploading it to SoundCloud before posting it on YouTube. The track didn't attract much attention at first, but it had reached around 125,000 views after four years.
Last summer, after noticing an increase in comments on the video, Shokin discovered that DJs were sampling her voice and using it in dozens of songs.
"The first thing that comes to mind is, 'Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn't credit me,'" she said.
Shokin later realized that the DJs had purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters, and her track was part of its "Folk Legends" set.
After she contacted the distributor, it apologized, assured her it was unaware of what had happened, and arranged royalties.
"I didn't love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation," she said.
Then, in October, her original YouTube video disappeared following a copyright complaint from a company called Media Nov Records. Shokin filed two counter-notifications, arguing that the video should stay up or not be demonetized, but they failed, and her attempts to contact the company went unanswered.
Media Nov Records is described as a "distribution company" that helps artists get their tracks onto digital platforms, but 404 Media notes that a lot of its website is focused on management and copyright protection.
"Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve," it reads. There's also mention of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition.
Media Nov told 404 Media it operates 500 channels. The outlet found AI imagery and repetitive electronic music across those it examined. Corporate records placed the company's founding last year, despite its website claiming roots in 1996.
Media Nov responded after 404 Media contacted it, initially saying it would investigate the claim and correct any error. It then contacted Shokin, requesting original audio files, recording evidence, publication dates, and other documentation proving ownership. The company blamed its failure to answer earlier messages from Shokin and Loopmasters on its spam folder.
It also brought Bulgarian composer Philip Koutev into the dispute. "Regarding 'Bre Petrunko,' we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev's work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content," the company told Shokin in an email.
Koutev popularized an arrangement of the traditional folk song in 1963. However, Media Nov did not answer when 404 Media asked which work in its catalog had triggered the complaint against Shokin.
Minutes after requesting proof of ownership, Media Nov emailed both Shokin and the publication to withdraw its removal request. Its bizarre explanation was that the video had "not generated revenue or received views," despite having accumulated around 125,000 views.
The company nevertheless maintained that it was not surrendering any rights, adding: "We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute."
Around 24 hours later, Shokin's video returned. YouTube confirmed it had restored the recording because the claimant withdrew its complaint.
"It's ironic that they're in the copyright business," Shokin said. "It's not the arrangement that's in question. It's the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they're talking about."
AI music has already brought plenty of problems beyond questionable copyright claims. Platforms are being overwhelmed with fully AI-generated tracks, many of which are fraudulent. Australia is banning them from the charts, and despite Spotify deleting millions of these tracks, it is introducing an AI remixing tool for users next year.

report.summary: An AI-driven copyright enforcement company falsely claimed ownership of a musician's own folk recording, got her YouTube video taken down, then withdrew the claim once pressed for proof.
report.background: Content ID and automated DMCA takedown systems were built to help rights holders police mass infringement at scale, but they assume the claimant actually owns the work. As generative AI floods streaming platforms with synthetic tracks, a parallel industry of 'rights management' firms has emerged that uses AI-powered audio recognition and bulk channel networks to file claims en masse, sometimes with little verification. The burden falls on creators, who must file counter-notifications and prove they own their own recordings while the claimant stays anonymous. Music sampling culture adds another layer: royalty-free sample packs resell recordings, and distributors may not always vet the source material. Meanwhile, platforms are struggling with AI slop, fraudulent streams, and chart manipulation, and countries like Australia are moving to ban fully AI-generated tracks from charts.
key_points: Samantha Shokin's 50-second Bulgarian folk recording was uploaded during the pandemic and grew to about 125,000 views. DJs later sampled her voice from a Loopmasters 'Folk Legends' pack. The distributor apologized, admitted it was unaware of the source, and paid royalties — a messy but resolvable sampling dispute.

In October, an AI-focused firm called Media Nov Records filed a copyright complaint that removed Shokin's original YouTube video. She filed two counter-notifications arguing the video should stay up or at least not be demonetized. Both failed, and the company ignored her messages until a journalist got involved.

Corporate records show Media Nov was founded last year despite a website claiming roots in 1996. It told 404 Media it operates 500 channels, and those examined contained AI imagery and repetitive electronic music. Its site advertises automated DMCA takedowns, Content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition.

When pressed, Media Nov demanded Shokin's original audio files, recording evidence, and publication dates to prove ownership — then withdrew its removal request minutes later. Its stated reason was that the video had 'not generated revenue or received views,' despite roughly 125,000 views, while insisting it retained its rights.

YouTube restored the video about 24 hours later after the claimant withdrew. Shokin noted the irony: the dispute was never about the folk arrangement or composition, but about her specific voice and performance, which the claimant appeared not to understand.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a credibility test. Firms selling 'AI-powered content recognition' and automated enforcement are only as trustworthy as their verification pipelines, and a single false claim can chill creators while the claimant faces no cost. For developers, it highlights a real engineering gap: matching audio fingerprints without confirming ownership, provenance, or the difference between a composition and a sound recording. Tools that timestamp, hash, and log original uploads could become standard hygiene. For regular users and artists, the lesson is blunt — automated claims can outpace human review, counter-notices may go nowhere, and press attention is often faster than the appeals process. Platforms will face growing pressure to penalize bad-faith claimants.
report.tools: Creators wanting protection can look at provenance and timestamping tools like Bernstein, OriginStamp, and Creative Commons licensing metadata, plus archival uploads to the Internet Archive. For fingerprinting and rights research, WhoSampled and Audible Magic's recognition services are worth knowing. YouTube's Content ID dispute and counter-notification flow, and the Copyright Alliance's DMCA guides, explain the appeals process. Following 404 Media's coverage of AI music and rights-management firms helps track emerging abuse patterns.
